title: Diagnosing Generalization Boundaries in AI-Based Vulnerability Detection via Calibrated Embedding Distances

paper.title: Diagnosing Generalization Boundaries in AI-Based Vulnerability Detection via Calibrated Embedding Distances
paper.abstract: Abstract. High benchmark scores in learning-based vulnerability detection mask severe degradation under distribution shifts. This paper demonstrates that calibrated embedding geometry exposes these hidden generalization boundaries on syntactically similar vulnerable and patched code pairs. An evaluation of CodeBERT and Qwen2.5-Coder across pattern, project, and temporal shifts on a strictly paired dataset reveals three main findings. First, whitened intermediate-layer embeddings with local nearest-neighbour scoring separate unfamiliar samples with a mean out-of-distribution AUROC of 0.739 (RQ1). Second, distance scores reveal a shift-specific reliability gradient where accuracy drops by over 35 percentage points and cross-project shifts cause the sharpest degradation, even though temporal shifts drift geometrically farthest (RQ2). Third, false positives on patched code systematically correlate with geometric proximity to vulnerable training neighbourhoods, increasing from 9.4% in the lowest-risk decile to 58.8% in the highest (RQ3). These calibrated distances establish a diagnostic signal that maps representation geometry directly to model degradation without requiring auxiliary models.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Alongside traditional static analysis, automated software vulnerability detection increasingly incorporates learning-based techniques ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) . In particular, transformer-based code models and Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong benchmark performance, with recent contributions demonstrating the efficacy of fine-tuned code models for security-patch and vulnerability analysis in industrial settings ( Ran et al., 2025 ) . These models process source code directly and adapt to security-specific classification via fine-tuning ( Shestov et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) , suggesting they capture recurring vulnerability patterns that are difficult to express through manual rules. However, strong benchmark performance does not guarantee reliable generalization beyond the training distribution. Many evaluations rely on in-distribution test sets sharing similar projects, coding styles, time periods, and vulnerability patterns. Under such conditions, models often exploit recurring superficial cues rather than learning robust vulnerability semantics ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) , causing detection performance to degrade on unfamiliar projects, later vulnerability instances, or unseen code structures that differ from the training distribution ( Li et al., 2026 ) . This raises a central question: where do the generalization boundaries of these models lie? Model predictions are only actionable if there is some indication of whether a model operates in a familiar region of its input space ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . For security applications, operating outside these boundaries is problematic because both missed vulnerabilities and false alarms carry severe operational costs. A particularly challenging scenario involves hard-negative samples that are difficult to distinguish from positive instances due to high semantic and structural similarity ( Robinson et al., 2021 ) . In this study, we operationalize this concept using vulnerable functions and their corresponding patched counterparts as software evolution artifacts. Such pairs share most tokens, control structures, and context, differing only in localized, security-relevant edits ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) . Unlike arbitrary benign code where models often exploit superficial shortcuts ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) , hard-negative pairs enforce a stricter evaluation of whether the model captures genuine vulnerability semantics. Ideally, an embedding space should organize code fragments by security semantics. In practice, however, vulnerable and patched snippets often cluster closely due to syntactic overlap, while out-of-distribution (OOD) samples drift far from training neighbourhoods (Figure 1 ). Moreover, at the local level this geometric overlap can trap samples within opposing neighbourhoods, most critically pulling safe patches into vulnerable clusters to trigger false alarms (Figure 2 ). Standard aggregate metrics reflect overall correctness, but fail to diagnose either phenomenon. This paper investigates generalization boundaries through embedding-based distance metrics, hypothesizing that geometric proximity to the training distribution provides a diagnostic reliability signal ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2022 ) . While contextual transformer representations generally suffer from inherent anisotropy ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) , local neighbourhood structures can capture vulnerability similarity in code ( Shimmi et al., 2024 ) . Yet, whether calibrated embedding geometry reliably exposes model failure boundaries under hard-negative and OOD shifts has remained an open challenge that we resolve in this work. To systematically examine this, an encoder (CodeBERT) and a generative LLM (Qwen2.5-Coder) are evaluated across controlled shift scenarios guided by three research questions: • RQ1 (Embedding Space Calibration): Which representation choices improve the separability of in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples in the embedding space? • RQ2 (Generalization Boundaries): To what extent do embedding-based distance metrics reveal generalization boundaries, and how do these boundaries behave under specific distribution shifts? • RQ3 (Vulnerable-Neighbourhood Proximity): To what extent are false positives on patched hard-negatives characterized by geometric proximity to vulnerable training neighbourhoods? By addressing these questions, this paper makes three main contributions: • A paired hard-negative ID/OOD benchmark. We construct an open, leakage-free dataset of strictly paired vulnerable and patched C/C++ functions partitioned across controlled pattern, project, and temporal shifts, preventing models from exploiting superficial shortcuts. • Distance-based generalization boundaries. We demonstrate that model degradation correlates directly with representation distance, showing that calibrated intermediate embeddings expose a continuous reliability gradient where accuracy drops by over 35 percentage points toward chance level under distribution shift. • Geometric diagnostics and test-time triage. We identify local neighbourhood entrapment as a primary driver of false alarms on repaired code and demonstrate that proximity to vulnerable training clusters provides an actionable signal to flag uncertain alerts before reaching developers. sections.heading: 2. Dataset and Experimental Design
sections.text: This section outlines the empirical foundation and experimental design. To analyze generalization boundaries effectively, the dataset must provide reliable vulnerability–patch relations, detailed project metadata, and controlled conditions for distribution shift evaluation. Mining vulnerability data directly from repositories introduces risks such as label noise, non-atomic commits, duplicate samples, and incomplete mappings ( Croft et al., 2023 ) . Such artifacts can lead to overly optimistic evaluations, causing models to learn dataset-specific shortcuts rather than vulnerability-relevant semantics ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) . To prevent this, the present study relies on a curated data foundation combining modern vulnerability datasets with explicit pair information. sections.heading: 2.1. Data Foundation and Hard-Negative Design
sections.text: The dataset is constructed from three complementary sources: PrimeVul ( Ding et al., 2025 ) , TitanVul ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and VulGate ( Safdar et al., 2026 ) . This multi-source foundation provides curated labels, explicit vulnerability–patch relations, and the metadata required for controlled distribution shift evaluation. To prevent the representation space from becoming sparse, the dataset is restricted to a semantically coherent subset of memory- and resource-safety vulnerabilities based on their Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) classes (e.g., CWE-119, CWE-416, CWE-787). Where project information is incomplete, metadata enrichment is performed using the National Vulnerability Database ( National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2024 ) . By design, the dataset is constructed exclusively from matched vulnerable and patched functions, yielding a balanced foundation of 12,190 initial pairs. We deliberately exclude arbitrary benign code. Unrelated benign samples introduce distributional disparities that encourage shortcut learning ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) , where models exploit superficial cues such as project-specific identifiers, coding styles, or function complexity rather than genuine flaws ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) . Evaluating strictly against patched counterparts forces models to distinguish the localized security edit rather than relying on repository artifacts ( Robinson et al., 2021 ; Xiao et al., 2020 ) , aligning with paired evaluation paradigms recently explored in vulnerability benchmarking across code patches and agent protocols ( Tang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 2.2. Data Cleaning and Normalization
sections.text: Transformer-based models typically process a fixed maximum token sequence. Simple truncation of long functions can inadvertently remove the vulnerability’s root cause from the model input ( Rahman and Hossen, 2023 ) . To address this, a character-level safety threshold of 1,500 characters is applied. If a pair exceeds this limit, pair-aligned multi-hunk extraction isolates the line-level differences alongside up to eight lines of surrounding context. Keeping all changed regions prevents the loss of disjoint security edits ( Nashid et al., 2025 ) and aligns with patch analysis principles, which emphasize that capturing localized security modifications alongside their immediate syntactic context is essential to preserve semantic consistency across disjoint edits ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . While real-world deployment requires scanning full functions without advance knowledge of patches, evaluating full functions directly under a 512-token limit risks discarding the vulnerability root cause entirely ( Rahman and Hossen, 2023 ) . Pair-aligned hunk reduction accepts a controlled granularity shift in order to guarantee that models are evaluated strictly on their ability to recognize the localized security delta, rather than being penalized by arbitrary tokenizer clipping artifacts. Following the preprocessing protocol of MCL-VD ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , inline and block comments are stripped, and pairs that become empty or identical after cleaning are removed. Subsequently, hash-based deduplication is applied at the pair level. If either side of a pair duplicates an existing snippet, the entire pair is discarded. This prevents data leakage and ensures models are evaluated on genuinely unseen samples ( Allamanis, 2019 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Finally, split-eligibility audits verify that all retained pairs have complete project, temporal, and diff-cluster metadata required for partition assignment, yielding a final dataset of 8,065 verified pairs. To guarantee absolute comparability, both the CodeBERT encoder and the Qwen2.5-Coder LLM are trained and evaluated on this exact same set of normalized inputs.

sections.heading: 2.3. Controlled Evaluation Groups
sections.text: Conventional random splits often overestimate generalization because training and test sets share projects, time periods, and recurring fix patterns. To isolate the exact causes of model failure, the dataset is partitioned hierarchically into five distinct evaluation groups. All splits maintain strict pair-level integrity, meaning a vulnerability and its corresponding patch are always assigned to the same group. To approximate familiarity with recurring vulnerability-fix patterns, patch-diff clusters are generated within each CWE class using MiniBatch K-Means on character-level TF-IDF features of the modified lines. Clustering the isolated diffs rather than full functions is essential: full-function representations would primarily group code by project style, variable naming, or surrounding framework context. In contrast, line-level diffs isolate the syntactic modification (e.g., operator adjustments, pointer validations) that resolves the flaw. Character-level n-grams are chosen because security patches often comprise short syntactic tokens, boundary operators, and numeric bounds rather than descriptive natural language. Furthermore, clustering is partitioned strictly per CWE with adaptive cluster budgets (e.g., 104 clusters for CWE-119 vs. 17 for CWE-415), preventing artificial over-fragmentation in sparse weakness categories while accounting for the heterogeneity of broader classes. The test set (845 pairs) is then structured as follows: • Random ID (28.2%) A conventional held-out baseline drawn from the remaining in-distribution pool. • Seen-Pattern ID (18.9%) Unseen pairs whose CWE classes and specific patch-diff clusters were already observed during training. • Same-CWE New-Pattern OOD (21.1%) Isolates pattern-level generalization. The CWE class is known, but the specific patch-diff cluster is entirely withheld from training. • Project OOD (17.5%) Measures cross-project robustness by withholding complete repositories (e.g. krb5, postgres) from training ( Steenhoek et al., 2023 ) . • Temporal OOD (14.3%) Isolates later Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records (disclosed in 2024) to simulate future deployment and prevent temporal leakage ( Jimenez et al., 2019 ) . Evaluation groups are extracted through a strict priority cascade that withholds full projects first, then temporal CVEs from the remaining data, and finally unseen pattern clusters. This sequential partitioning prevents samples from satisfying multiple holdout conditions simultaneously, with automated checks verifying zero leakage across splits.

sections.heading: 2.4. Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Due to the balanced paired design, Accuracy serves as the primary classification metric, complemented by the F1 score. Because the negative class consists exclusively of repaired code, the Patch False-Positive Rate (Patch-FPR) is explicitly evaluated. A high Patch-FPR indicates that the model frequently flags repaired code as vulnerable, failing to recognize the security fix. Symmetrically, the False-Negative Rate (FNR) measures the proportion of genuine vulnerabilities that the model misses. For OOD detection and distance-based risk, the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) is used. Each sample receives a continuous distance score reflecting its geometric displacement from the training ID Core toward unfamiliar OOD regions (Fig. 1 ), formally defined in Section 3.3 . AUROC evaluates the score’s ability to rank unfamiliar samples or incorrect predictions higher than familiar ones, independent of an operational threshold ( Fawcett, 2006 ) .

sections.heading: 3. Methodology
sections.text: The experimental design evaluates embedding calibration, OOD scoring, and cross-model failure prediction. We examine two distinct model families, namely the CodeBERT encoder and the Qwen2.5-Coder language model. To isolate how task-specific training alters latent geometry compared to raw pretraining, we evaluate CodeBERT in both its original pretrained state and after fine-tuning with a joint cross-entropy and contrastive objective. The encoder produces fixed-dimensional embeddings for distance-based OOD scoring, while Qwen2.5-Coder acts as an independent generative classifier. This configuration allows us to test cross-model transfer, determining whether geometric distance scores derived from a lightweight encoder can reliably warn of prediction failures in a separate large language model.

sections.heading: 3.1. Model and Training Setup
sections.text: The encoder architecture is based on CodeBERT ( microsoft/codebert-base ) ( Feng et al., 2020 ) . A central challenge in hard-negative vulnerability detection is that a vulnerable function and its patched counterpart share extensive syntactic overlap, yet a standard cross-entropy objective does not explicitly enforce geometric separation between their latent representations. To address this, the encoder is fine-tuned with a joint Cross-Entropy (CE) and Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL) objective ( Gunel et al., 2021 ; Khosla et al., 2020 ) . We adapted the contrastive loss formulation from framework implementations such as SCL-CVD and MCL-VD ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . Unlike approaches that fuse Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), control-flow graphs, or synthesized comments to optimize raw benchmark metrics, we restrict our encoder to unimodal source code. This eliminates parsing artifacts and confounders from external static analyzers, ensuring that observed geometric boundaries and neighbourhood structures directly reflect the latent properties of the contextualized language model itself. Following common practice in contrastive learning, the temperature is set to τ = 0.07 \tau=0.07 ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Khosla et al., 2020 ) , while, following the objective-balancing principles of Gunel et al. ( Gunel et al., 2021 ) and SCL-CVD ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , the scaling weight is set to λ = 0.05 \lambda=0.05 . Training utilizes pair-complete mini-batches containing four exact vulnerable-patch pairs. This operationalizes contrastive hard-negative principles ( Robinson et al., 2021 ) by guaranteeing that the most informative counterpart, namely the repaired patch ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) , is present in every optimization step despite the hardware-constrained batch size. Both encoder variants are adapted with LoRA ( r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 , dropout 0.1 0.1 , applied to query, key, value, and dense projection modules) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , building on recent empirical evidence showing that parameter-efficient adaptation preserves foundational representations while effectively capturing code task semantics ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . The final three transformer layers are additionally unfrozen, preserving general pretrained structure in lower layers while enabling task-specific abstraction in upper layers ( Lee et al., 2019 ) . As a cross-model reliability baseline, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct ( Hui et al., 2024 ) is adapted as a sequence classifier via QLoRA (4-bit NF4, r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 , dropout 0.05 0.05 ) ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Shestov et al., 2025 ) . The model input consists of a specific task instruction followed directly by the C or C++ code snippet: “Analyze the following C/C++ code and determine if it contains a vulnerability.” A binary classification head is applied to the final non-padding token of this combined sequence at the output layer. The LLM is fine-tuned using standard cross-entropy loss, where a pair-preserving sampler places vulnerable and patched counterparts within the same mini-batch to ensure balanced gradient updates across identical project contexts.

sections.heading: 3.2. Embedding Extraction & Calibration
sections.text: Embeddings are extracted from the [CLS] token ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) at every transformer layer (0–12) and as aggregated layer means. Layer choice is treated as an empirical factor because prior probing work shows a functional progression where lower layers encode general syntax, while higher layers specialize toward the training objective ( Tenney et al., 2019 ) . A final layer tightly specialized for CE classification may lose the broader distributional structure required for OOD ranking. Raw contextualized embeddings suffer from inherent anisotropy, clustering within a narrow cone of dominant directions ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) . In hard-negative vulnerability detection, where a function and its patch often differ by merely a few tokens (e.g., an added boundary check), this geometric distortion is critical: high-variance dimensions corresponding to surface syntax or project-specific identifier naming drown out the subtle semantic delta of the actual fix. To restore metric expressiveness, we apply a whitening transformation ( Su et al., 2021 ) that centers and decorrelates the training distribution via the empirical covariance 𝚺 = 𝐔 ​ 𝚲 ​ 𝐔 ⊤ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^{\top} : 𝐖 = ( 𝚲 + ϵ 𝐈 ) − 1 / 2 𝐔 ⊤ , 𝐳 white ( x ) = 𝐖 ( 𝐡 ( x ) − 𝝁 ) \mathbf{W}=(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}+\epsilon\mathbf{I})^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{white}}(x)=\mathbf{W}\bigl(\mathbf{h}(x)-\boldsymbol{\mu}\bigr) where 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} is the training mean vector and ϵ = 10 − 5 \epsilon=10^{-5} is a numerical regularizer. By equalizing eigenvalue variance across all feature dimensions, whitening prevents generic code structure from dominating cosine similarity, allowing localized repair semantics to govern latent distances.

sections.heading: 3.3. Distance-Based OOD Scoring
sections.text: Vulnerability data is multi-modal, with different CWE classes, projects, and patch patterns occupying distinct local regions in the embedding space. Consequently, OOD scoring is operationalized using a non-parametric k k -nearest-neighbour cosine distance to the training distribution ( Sun et al., 2022 ) . Let E ⁡ ( x ) E(x) denote the calibrated embedding of sample x x under a given transformation (e.g., E ​ ( x ) = 𝐳 white ​ ( x ) E(x)=\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{white}}(x) ), and let N k ​ ( x ) N_{k}(x) denote its set of k k nearest training neighbours under cosine similarity. The non-parametric outlier score is computed as: OOD k ​ ( x ) = 1 − 1 k ​ ∑ n i ∈ N k ​ ( x ) cos ⁡ ( E ⁡ ( x ) , E ⁡ ( n i ) ) \mathrm{OOD}_{k}(x)=1-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{n_{i}\in N_{k}(x)}\cos\bigl(E(x),\,E(n_{i})\bigr) The parameter k k is systematically swept across k ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 , 50 , 100 } k\in\{1,3,5,10,20,30,50,100\} . A diagonal approximation of the class-conditional Mahalanobis distance ( Lee et al., 2018 ) is included as a global parametric baseline. To evaluate whether distance scores expose a gradual generalization boundary, test samples are grouped into ten equal-frequency distance bins to compute accuracy and error rates. This is evaluated intrinsically (the encoder scored against its own predictions) and cross-model (using encoder-derived distances to rank LLM errors). Because neural networks can remain overconfident under distribution shift ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) , the LLM’s internal confidence (maximum softmax probability) ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ) is reported as a baseline. The analysis is repeated across shift types (in-distribution, unseen-pattern, cross-project, temporal), additionally measuring pair-exact correctness to assess whether both sides of a hard-negative pair are successfully identified.

sections.heading: 3.4. Vulnerable-Neighbourhood Proximity
sections.text: A specific hard-negative failure mode occurs when a patched function remains geometrically closer to vulnerable training examples than to safe counterparts, leading to misclassification. To investigate this, we analyze patched test samples using the fine-tuned CE+SCL encoder, contrasting patched false positives (predicted vulnerable) against patched true negatives (predicted patched). The contrastive objective makes this neighbourhood-based analysis directly interpretable by explicitly shaping class-wise structure ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) . To examine how test samples interact with the underlying training distribution, proximity to the vulnerable class is quantified using four complementary metrics in the calibrated embedding space. These include a centroid margin ratio, a nearest-neighbour margin, a class-conditional k k -neighbourhood margin ratio ( k = 10 k=10 ), and the vulnerable-neighbour share among the top 10 neighbours illustrated in Fig. 2 . Grounded in neighbourhood-based prediction support and embedding similarity ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ; Shimmi et al., 2024 ) , class-conditional density estimation ( Lee et al., 2018 ) , and internal-state risk assessment ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , these metrics measure whether a patch is drawn toward the vulnerable or the safe training distribution. We assess their diagnostic value by comparing group means with 95% confidence intervals, ranking false alarms via AUROC, and evaluating risk gradients across proximity deciles.

This aligns with prior findings that distinguishing vulnerabilities from their patches is considerably harder than standard classification ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) , where models often rely on superficial dataset cues rather than genuine defect semantics ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) . Qwen2.5-Coder-7B achieves the strongest test accuracy and F1 score, but its margin over CodeBERT CE+SCL remains modest despite larger model capacity. At the same time, the patch false-positive rate remains consistently high across all models, demonstrating that classifiers capture vulnerable context while failing to verify whether the defect was repaired. While Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL) yields substantial gains in vision and NLP, its impact on raw binary classification here remains constrained. The bottleneck lies in the extreme syntactic overlap of hard-negative pairs: while SCL does not noticeably improve global OOD ranking over the raw encoder (RQ1), it successfully structures the latent space for local, class-conditional diagnostics of patched false positives (RQ3), even though translating this realignment into a superior linear decision boundary remains challenging.

sections.heading: 4.1. RQ1: Embedding Space Calibration
sections.text: RQ1 investigates representation choices for separating in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, measured by mean OOD-AUROC across the three OOD conditions. The strongest overall configuration across the grid uses raw pretrained CodeBERT at layer 3 with whitening and k = 1 k=1 , achieving a mean OOD-AUROC of 0.739. Notably, this best geometry stems from the raw encoder rather than fine-tuned variants (which peak at 0.735 for CE+SCL), indicating that fine-tuning optimizes decision boundaries at the expense of broader OOD geometry. Post-whitening L2 normalization yielded identical results, hence only whitening is reported.

sections.heading: Effect of Embedding Transformation
sections.text: Raw embeddings with cosine nearest-neighbour scoring reach a best mean OOD-AUROC of 0.710, whereas whitened variants reach 0.739 (Table 2 ), confirming that decorrelating dominant variance directions restores metric utility. The failure of the diagonal Mahalanobis baseline (best mean 0.547) underscores that code repositories and CWE mechanisms form a fragmented multi-modal manifold rather than a single Gaussian cluster. Consequently, distance scoring strictly favors local nearest neighbours ( k = 1 k=1 achieves 0.739, as shown later in Table 4 ), as snippets are familiar if they match even a single recurring implementation pattern in training. sections.heading: 4.2. RQ2: Generalization Boundaries
sections.text: RQ2 investigates whether embedding-based distance exposes a reliability gradient and whether this gradient behaves uniformly across distribution shifts. All following analyses use the layer-3 whitened configuration ( k = 1 k=1 ) identified in RQ1. For interpretability, the test set is divided into ten equal-frequency distance bins (169 samples each) wherever a bin-level analysis is reported.

sections.heading: Encoder-Intrinsic and Cross-Model Boundaries
sections.text: Figure 4 shows CodeBERT CE+SCL performance over its own embedding distance. A clear degradation pattern emerges. Accuracy falls from 0.834 in the lowest-distance bin to 0.479 in the highest, which is a drop of more than 35 percentage points, while the patch false-positive rate rises from 0.167 to 0.631. Converting prediction correctness into a binary error indicator, the resulting error-ranking AUROC is 0.593 (Spearman r = 0.157 r=0.157 ). This confirms a modest but meaningful reliability signal consistent with the large accuracy drop (full ten-bin results available in the online replication package). Operationally, this geometric gradient enables prediction and risk-aware triage in software security pipelines. By grouping distance bins into empirical zones—Safe (Bins 1–3), Boundary (Bins 4–6), and Danger (Bins 7–10)—a system can selectively abstain from fully automated decisions on distant code. Abstaining on samples in the highest-distance Danger Zone yields 71.6% accuracy on the retained low-distance code (Safe Zone) compared to 53.4% in the rejected region (Danger Zone), while reducing the false alarm rate on safe code down to 33.7%. To evaluate whether this geometric signal transfers across model families, Figure 5 uses raw CodeBERT distance to rank errors made by the independently fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder LLM. LLM accuracy decreases from 0.680 to 0.539 across distance bins, while mean confidence declines only slightly from ≈ \approx 0.81 to ≈ \approx 0.78. This reproduces the known overconfidence of neural networks under distribution shift ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . While the cross-model error-ranking AUROC (0.556) is weaker than the encoder-intrinsic setting, it remains consistently above random ranking. CodeBERT distance and LLM confidence thus capture complementary reliability aspects: confidence reflects internal certainty, while distance provides an external measure of distributional proximity. sections.text: Figure 6 relates distributional displacement to classification degradation across the evaluation groups. The two in-distribution baselines remain clustered in lower distance regions ( ≈ \approx 0.49), while pattern and project shifts displace samples outward ( ≈ \approx 0.65). Across shifts, geometric distance and classification degradation decouple. Temporal samples are geometrically farthest from the training distribution, yet CE+SCL encoder accuracy on temporal samples (0.574) exceeds that on the project group (0.517). The project group represents the most severe failure mode overall, suffering the lowest accuracy alongside the highest false-positive rate (0.507), meaning more than half of all patched cross-project samples are misclassified as vulnerable. Temporal shift instead produces the highest false-negative rate (0.455). This demonstrates that high distance is a necessary but not sufficient condition for severe degradation. The structural nature of the shift determines how displacement translates into specific failure modes. This non-linear divergence is grounded in representation geometry. While temporal shift induces a uniform distributional drift away from the training corpus across all classes, cross-project shift causes severe representation entanglement. As neighbourhood diagnostics reveal (detailed in the supplementary package), cross-project patched samples are the only evaluation group exhibiting a positive group-level centroid vulnerability margin (+0.016, detailed in the supplementary repository). Unseen repository conventions, custom macros, and unfamiliar API patterns do not merely push samples outward—they actively displace safe patches into the geometric sphere of vulnerable training clusters, triggering systematic false alarms (see supplementary material).

sections.heading: Hard-Negative Pair Behaviour
sections.text: Evaluating the same shifts at the level of strictly vulnerable–patched pairs exposes a more severe failure picture (Figure 7 ). Even in the combined in-distribution setting, only 39.5% of pairs are classified exactly correctly (where both the vulnerability and its patch are identified correctly). For an independent binary classifier, predicting both sides of a pair correctly yields an expected random baseline of 25% ( 0.5 × 0.5 0.5\times 0.5 ). Under OOD shifts, pair-exact correctness consistently drops below this threshold: 22.5% for unseen patterns, 19.8% for temporal shifts, and 18.9% across projects. This demonstrates that models under shift do not merely degrade gradually, but systematically misclassify the localized repair delta. These shift-specific paired error profiles are invisible at the sample level, confirming that pair-aware evaluation is essential for hard-negative reliability. Figure 7. sections.heading: CWE-Level Failure Modes
sections.text: Beyond shift type, generalization boundaries depend heavily on the specific vulnerability class. Table 5 reports performance per CWE for the CE+SCL encoder (full class breakdown in supplementary repository). CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) is the most robust class with the highest accuracy (0.722). In contrast, CWE-416 (Use After Free) is the weakest overall (accuracy 0.542) despite substantial training support (1,636 samples) and a moderate mean OOD distance (0.566). This indicates that poor performance is intrinsic to the semantic complexity of the class rather than a pure distance effect. The dominant error type also varies across classes. CWE-415 (Double Free) suffers from a severe false-negative rate (0.528), plausibly compounded by limited training support. Conversely, CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference) reaches the highest mean OOD distance (0.659) alongside a high false-positive rate (0.483). sections.heading: 5. Discussion
sections.text: The results support the argument that calibrated embedding distances make generalization boundaries empirically observable, while revealing qualifications about when and how this signal is useful.

sections.heading: Classification Performance and Representation Geometry
sections.text: The decoupling between classification accuracy and OOD separability observed in RQ1 suggests that fine-tuning reshapes the embedding space toward the classification boundary at the expense of the broader distributional structure needed for reliable OOD ranking ( Kumar et al., 2022 ) . This decoupling carries direct architectural implications for secure software engineering pipelines. Standard practice assumes that safety checks and confidence scores should originate from the final layer of the active classifier. Our findings demonstrate that task fine-tuning forces an objective-driven feature collapse in upper layers (10–12) to linearly separate labels, destroying the broader contextual variance required for OOD scoring. Synthesizing these layer dynamics with our cross-model transfer results in RQ2, production security tools should adopt a dual-representation architecture. A high-capacity classifier such as a fine-tuned LLM performs primary vulnerability triage, while an auxiliary, frozen intermediate encoder representation (CodeBERT Layer 3 with whitening) operates as an independent guardrail to flag out-of-distribution inputs. This dual architecture adds negligible latency to the screening pipeline. With 125M parameters, the frozen CodeBERT encoder is over 50 times smaller than a 7B LLM and computes distance scores in under 5 ms per function, allowing security tools to screen code before invoking resource-heavy generative inference or manual triage.

sections.heading: Distance-Based Boundaries and Model Dependence
sections.text: That LLM confidence remains comparatively high even as accuracy declines with distance is consistent with broader evidence that neural-network confidence is poorly calibrated and degrades further under distribution shift ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . This non-redundancy has a direct practical consequence: a system relying on model confidence alone would fail to flag exactly the high-distance region where CodeBERT-derived distance proves informative.

sections.heading: Shift-Specific and Geometric Failure Modes
sections.text: The RQ3 proximity analysis offers a representation-level account of why cross-project shift is harder than its distance alone would predict ( Steenhoek et al., 2023 ) : it is the only evaluation group whose patched samples are geometrically closer to the vulnerable class centroid than to the patched class. While prior work established that representation geometry and neighbour embeddings capture vulnerability similarity ( Shimmi et al., 2024 ) , our findings ground shift-induced failures directly in this geometry, confirming that these errors reflect measurable shortcut learning ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Vulnerability-Class-Dependent Failure Modes
sections.text: The CWE-level results show that vulnerability semantics shape the generalization boundary beyond distance and shift type. CWE-416 remains the weakest class despite substantial training support, suggesting that lifetime and aliasing relations are difficult to recover from short truncated snippets. CWE-415 shows a similar false-negative pattern, whereas CWE-787 and CWE-120 appear more robust because their signals are more locally observable. Overall, lifetime- and control-flow-dependent weaknesses likely require representations beyond token-level context.

sections.heading: Construct Validity
sections.text: Using vulnerable–patched pairs isolates the security delta but omits arbitrary benign code common in deployment. Furthermore, while hunk extraction ensures the root cause fits within the model’s context window, real-world tools must inspect entire functions where the vulnerability location is unknown a priori . Finally, patch-diff clusters provide an automated operational proxy for fix categories rather than manually validated semantic taxonomies.

sections.heading: Internal Validity
sections.text: Pair integrity, leakage prevention, and duplicate removal strengthen internal validity. Source datasets may contain label noise or non-security refactoring changes within patches, influencing both classification and distance. The character-level input limit and hunk extraction mitigate arbitrary tokenizer truncation but may remove broader function context relevant to specific vulnerabilities. Additionally, RQ2 and RQ3 condition their analyses on the strongest configuration identified in RQ1 (full parameter grid in supplementary material).

sections.heading: External Validity
sections.text: The dataset is restricted to seven memory and resource-safety CWE classes in C and C++. This supports controlled hard-negative analysis but limits generalization to web vulnerabilities, cryptographic misuse, or other programming languages. The evaluation relies on specific held-out projects and a 2024 temporal cutoff. The evaluated models are limited to CodeBERT and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. Results may differ for encoders with explicit data-flow inputs or significantly larger LLM variants.

sections.heading: Conclusion Validity
sections.text: Model comparisons rely on fixed training runs rather than extensive repeated-run studies. The conclusions emphasize consistent qualitative patterns across evaluation groups rather than minor absolute metric differences. The equal-frequency distance bins used for boundary analysis are empirical and dataset-dependent. Statistical association does not establish strict causality. Proximity to vulnerable neighbourhoods is a geometric contributor to patched false positives, but it interacts with local classifier thresholds, input truncation, and project context.

sections.heading: 6. Related Work
sections.text: The literature relevant to this study spans four areas.

sections.heading: Distribution Shift in Vulnerability Detection
sections.text: Chakraborty et al. ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) showed that deep detectors rely on shortcut features that fail under distribution shift. Jimenez et al. ( Jimenez et al., 2019 ) identified temporal leakage as a distinct cause, with recent studies confirming that LLMs continue to struggle under software evolution and dataset shifts over time ( Bhutamapuram et al., 2025 ) . Steenhoek et al. ( Steenhoek et al., 2023 ) isolated project identity as a further factor in model degradation, underscoring ongoing efforts to transition vulnerability benchmarks from isolated functions to realistic repository-level contexts ( Lbath, 2026 ) . Li et al. ( Li et al., 2026 ) confirmed in a controlled benchmark that in-distribution performance does not predict OOD generalization. These studies largely treat OOD code as a single undifferentiated category. The present work extends their methodology by systematically isolating pattern, project, and temporal shifts across all evaluations. Our RQ2 findings reveal that geometric distance and classification failure do not correlate linearly across shift categories, showing that project-level shift degrades model reliability far out of proportion to its distributional displacement.

sections.heading: Hard-Negative and Patch-Based Detection
sections.text: Xiao et al. ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) combined vulnerability and patch signatures in MVP to avoid flagging already-repaired code. While recent research focuses on prioritizing alerts and mitigating false alarms in automated tools ( Amusuo et al., 2026 ) , deep learning detectors themselves still suffer from high false-alarm rates when inspecting repaired functions. Fu and Tantithamthavorn ( Fu and Tantithamthavorn, 2022 ) showed with LineVul that vulnerability evidence is often confined to a few lines, explaining why patched functions form strict hard-negatives. In parallel, SCL-CVD and MCL-VD ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) pursue class separation via contrastive training, while Shimmi et al. ( Shimmi et al., 2024 ) and Papernot and McDaniel ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ) demonstrated that local neighbourhood structure carries diagnostic value. While prior research uses hard-negatives and neighbourhoods mainly as training or retrieval mechanisms, this paper applies them diagnostically. Our pair-exact evaluation confirms the concerns behind MVP directly, and our proximity analysis gives the shortcut behaviour anticipated by prior work a concrete geometric signature.

sections.heading: Contextual Embedding Geometry
sections.text: Ethayarajh ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) established that contextual embeddings are inherently anisotropic. Su et al. ( Su et al., 2021 ) and Huang et al. ( Huang et al., 2021 ) showed that whitening restores distance as a meaningful similarity measure for sentence embeddings, and Tenney et al. ( Tenney et al., 2019 ) demonstrated via edge probing that transformer layers specialize progressively with depth. The findings in RQ1 confirm these concepts jointly for code representations. Whitening effectively corrects for anisotropy, while the layer-wise analysis extends depth progression to an OOD setting. Our results show that the last-layer specialization described in prior work comes at a direct cost to the broader distributional structure required for reliable distance-based analysis.

sections.heading: OOD Detection and Model Calibration
sections.text: Hendrycks and Gimpel ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ) established maximum softmax probability as an OOD baseline. Guo et al. ( Guo et al., 2017 ) showed modern networks are poorly calibrated, and Ovadia et al. ( Ovadia et al., 2019 ) demonstrated this worsens under dataset shift. For geometric scoring, Lee et al. ( Lee et al., 2018 ) proposed a parametric class-conditional alternative, while Sun et al. ( Sun et al., 2022 ) proposed a non-parametric k k NN distance. Our calibration results confirm Sun et al.’s findings for code, demonstrating that the most useful OOD signal is local rather than global. Furthermore, the cross-model evaluation confirms the overconfidence problem for code-specific LLMs, showing that an externally calibrated encoder distance exposes reliability information that the LLM’s own confidence fails to capture, reinforcing findings on the unreliability of raw model confidence in software diagnostics ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: This study demonstrates that calibrated embedding distances make the generalization boundaries of vulnerability detection models empirically observable under hard-negative conditions. Scaling model capacity alone does not resolve hard-negative confusion, as generative LLMs remain vulnerable to the same localized syntax traps as smaller encoders. We show that whitened intermediate CodeBERT layers provide the strongest separation of familiar and unfamiliar code. Distance-based boundaries are gradual and shift-specific: cross-project shifts cause the sharpest accuracy drops, while temporal shifts push samples furthest from the training distribution, heavily inflating false negatives. Patched false positives systematically correlate with geometric proximity to vulnerable training neighbourhoods. Practical implications include the ability to retrofit existing security scanners directly with out-of-distribution scores derived from intermediate layers via post-hoc whitening. Because this transformation requires no gradient updates or separate shadow models, practitioners can introduce dynamic risk stratification into CI/CD pipelines with negligible compute overhead. This enables selective prediction: automated tools can confidently flag vulnerabilities in familiar code regions while routing geometrically distant or entangled functions to security analysts. Because error profiles are shift-dependent, distance scores indicate which operational trade-off to budget for: auditing unfamiliar repositories requires reviewer capacity to handle inflated false alarms, whereas inspecting temporally shifted code necessitates recall-focused monitoring against silently missed defects. Future work should extend this geometric framework beyond textual representations to graph- and data-flow-based models, which may better capture lifetime-dependent vulnerabilities such as Use-After-Free flaws. In addition, future research should explore explicit fine-tuning objectives tailored specifically to OOD density estimation rather than relying solely on cross-entropy classification, and validate boundary stability across multi-year longitudinal code evolution.

High benchmark scores in learning-based vulnerability detection mask severe degradation under distribution shifts. This paper demonstrates that calibrated embedding geometry exposes these hidden generalization boundaries on syntactically similar vulnerable and patched code pairs. An evaluation of CodeBERT and Qwen2.5-Coder across pattern, project, and temporal shifts on a strictly paired dataset reveals three main findings. First, whitened intermediate-layer embeddings with local nearest-neighbour scoring separate unfamiliar samples with a mean out-of-distribution AUROC of 0.739 (RQ1). Second, distance scores reveal a shift-specific reliability gradient where accuracy drops by over 35 percentage points and cross-project shifts cause the sharpest degradation, even though temporal shifts drift geometrically farthest (RQ2). Third, false positives on patched code systematically correlate with geometric proximity to vulnerable training neighbourhoods, increasing from 9.4% in the lowest-risk decile to 58.8% in the highest (RQ3). These calibrated distances establish a diagnostic signal that maps representation geometry directly to model degradation without requiring auxiliary models. Keywords: Vulnerability Detection, Deep Learning, Out-of-Distribution, Software Security, Hard-Negatives 1. Introduction Alongside traditional static analysis, automated software vulnerability detection increasingly incorporates learning-based techniques ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) . In particular, transformer-based code models and Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong benchmark performance, with recent contributions demonstrating the efficacy of fine-tuned code models for security-patch and vulnerability analysis in industrial settings ( Ran et al., 2025 ) . These models process source code directly and adapt to security-specific classification via fine-tuning ( Shestov et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) , suggesting they capture recurring vulnerability patterns that are difficult to express through manual rules. However, strong benchmark performance does not guarantee reliable generalization beyond the training distribution. Many evaluations rely on in-distribution test sets sharing similar projects, coding styles, time periods, and vulnerability patterns. Under such conditions, models often exploit recurring superficial cues rather than learning robust vulnerability semantics ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) , causing detection performance to degrade on unfamiliar projects, later vulnerability instances, or unseen code structures that differ from the training distribution ( Li et al., 2026 ) . This raises a central question: where do the generalization boundaries of these models lie? Model predictions are only actionable if there is some indication of whether a model operates in a familiar region of its input space ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . For security applications, operating outside these boundaries is problematic because both missed vulnerabilities and false alarms carry severe operational costs. A particularly challenging scenario involves hard-negative samples that are difficult to distinguish from positive instances due to high semantic and structural similarity ( Robinson et al., 2021 ) . In this study, we operationalize this concept using vulnerable functions and their corresponding patched counterparts as software evolution artifacts. Such pairs share most tokens, control structures, and context, differing only in localized, security-relevant edits ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) . Unlike arbitrary benign code where models often exploit superficial shortcuts ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) , hard-negative pairs enforce a stricter evaluation of whether the model captures genuine vulnerability semantics. Ideally, an embedding space should organize code fragments by security semantics. In practice, however, vulnerable and patched snippets often cluster closely due to syntactic overlap, while out-of-distribution (OOD) samples drift far from training neighbourhoods (Figure 1 ). Moreover, at the local level this geometric overlap can trap samples within opposing neighbourhoods, most critically pulling safe patches into vulnerable clusters to trigger false alarms (Figure 2 ). Standard aggregate metrics reflect overall correctness, but fail to diagnose either phenomenon. This paper investigates generalization boundaries through embedding-based distance metrics, hypothesizing that geometric proximity to the training distribution provides a diagnostic reliability signal ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2022 ) . While contextual transformer representations generally suffer from inherent anisotropy ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) , local neighbourhood structures can capture vulnerability similarity in code ( Shimmi et al., 2024 ) . Yet, whether calibrated embedding geometry reliably exposes model failure boundaries under hard-negative and OOD shifts has remained an open challenge that we resolve in this work. To systematically examine this, an encoder (CodeBERT) and a generative LLM (Qwen2.5-Coder) are evaluated across controlled shift scenarios guided by three research questions: • RQ1 (Embedding Space Calibration): Which representation choices improve the separability of in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples in the embedding space? • RQ2 (Generalization Boundaries): To what extent do embedding-based distance metrics reveal generalization boundaries, and how do these boundaries behave under specific distribution shifts? • RQ3 (Vulnerable-Neighbourhood Proximity): To what extent are false positives on patched hard-negatives characterized by geometric proximity to vulnerable training neighbourhoods? By addressing these questions, this paper makes three main contributions: • A paired hard-negative ID/OOD benchmark. We construct an open, leakage-free dataset of strictly paired vulnerable and patched C/C++ functions partitioned across controlled pattern, project, and temporal shifts, preventing models from exploiting superficial shortcuts. • Distance-based generalization boundaries. We demonstrate that model degradation correlates directly with representation distance, showing that calibrated intermediate embeddings expose a continuous reliability gradient where accuracy drops by over 35 percentage points toward chance level under distribution shift. • Geometric diagnostics and test-time triage. We identify local neighbourhood entrapment as a primary driver of false alarms on repaired code and demonstrate that proximity to vulnerable training clusters provides an actionable signal to flag uncertain alerts before reaching developers. Dataset and Experimental Design This section outlines the empirical foundation and experimental design. To analyze generalization boundaries effectively, the dataset must provide reliable vulnerability–patch relations, detailed project metadata, and controlled conditions for distribution shift evaluation. Mining vulnerability data directly from repositories introduces risks such as label noise, non-atomic commits, duplicate samples, and incomplete mappings ( Croft et al., 2023 ) . Such artifacts can lead to overly optimistic evaluations, causing models to learn dataset-specific shortcuts rather than vulnerability-relevant semantics ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) . To prevent this, the present study relies on a curated data foundation combining modern vulnerability datasets with explicit pair information. Data Foundation and Hard-Negative Design The dataset is constructed from three complementary sources: PrimeVul ( Ding et al., 2025 ) , TitanVul ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and VulGate ( Safdar et al., 2026 ) . This multi-source foundation provides curated labels, explicit vulnerability–patch relations, and the metadata required for controlled distribution shift evaluation. To prevent the representation space from becoming sparse, the dataset is restricted to a semantically coherent subset of memory- and resource-safety vulnerabilities based on their Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) classes (e.g., CWE-119, CWE-416, CWE-787). Where project information is incomplete, metadata enrichment is performed using the National Vulnerability Database ( National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2024 ) . By design, the dataset is constructed exclusively from matched vulnerable and patched functions, yielding a balanced foundation of 12,190 initial pairs. We deliberately exclude arbitrary benign code. Unrelated benign samples introduce distributional disparities that encourage shortcut learning ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) , where models exploit superficial cues such as project-specific identifiers, coding styles, or function complexity rather than genuine flaws ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ) . Evaluating strictly against patched counterparts forces models to distinguish the localized security edit rather than relying on repository artifacts ( Robinson et al., 2021 ; Xiao et al., 2020 ) , aligning with paired evaluation paradigms recently explored in vulnerability benchmarking across code patches and agent protocols ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . 2.2. Data Cleaning and Normalization Transformer-based models typically process a fixed maximum token sequence. Simple truncation of long functions can inadvertently remove the vulnerability’s root cause from the model input ( Rahman and Hossen, 2023 ) . To address this, a character-level safety threshold of 1,500 characters is applied. If a pair exceeds this limit, pair-aligned multi-hunk extraction isolates the line-level differences alongside up to eight lines of surrounding context. Keeping all changed regions prevents the loss of disjoint security edits ( Nashid et al., 2025 ) and aligns with patch analysis principles, which emphasize that capturing localized security modifications alongside their immediate syntactic context is essential to preserve semantic consistency across disjoint edits ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . While real-world deployment requires scanning full functions without advance knowledge of patches, evaluating full functions directly under a 512-token limit risks discarding the vulnerability root cause entirely ( Rahman and Hossen, 2023 ) . Pair-aligned hunk reduction accepts a controlled granularity shift in order to guarantee that models are evaluated strictly on their ability to recognize the localized security delta, rather than being penalized by arbitrary tokenizer clipping artifacts. Following the preprocessing protocol of MCL-VD ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , inline and block comments are stripped, and pairs that become empty or identical after cleaning are removed. Subsequently, hash-based deduplication is applied at the pair level. If either side of a pair duplicates an existing snippet, the entire pair is discarded. This prevents data leakage and ensures models are evaluated on genuinely unseen samples ( Allamanis, 2019 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Finally, split-eligibility audits verify that all retained pairs have complete project, temporal, and diff-cluster metadata required for partition assignment, yielding a final dataset of 8,065 verified pairs. To guarantee absolute comparability, both the CodeBERT encoder and the Qwen2.5-Coder LLM are trained and evaluated on this exact same set of normalized inputs. 2.3. Controlled Evaluation Groups Conventional random splits often overestimate generalization because training and test sets share projects, time periods, and recurring fix patterns. To isolate the exact causes of model failure, the dataset is partitioned hierarchically into five distinct evaluation groups. All splits maintain strict pair-level integrity, meaning a vulnerability and its corresponding patch are always assigned to the same group. To approximate familiarity with recurring vulnerability-fix patterns, patch-diff clusters are generated within each CWE class using MiniBatch K-Means on character-level TF-IDF features of the modified lines. Clustering the isolated diffs rather than full functions is essential: full-function representations would primarily group code by project style, variable naming, or surrounding framework context. In contrast, line-level diffs isolate the syntactic modification (e.g., operator adjustments, pointer validations) that resolves the flaw. Character-level n-grams are chosen because security patches often comprise short syntactic tokens, boundary operators, and numeric bounds rather than descriptive natural language. Furthermore, clustering is partitioned strictly per CWE with adaptive cluster budgets (e.g., 104 clusters for CWE-119 vs. 17 for CWE-415), preventing artificial over-fragmentation in sparse weakness categories while accounting for the heterogeneity of broader classes. The test set (845 pairs) is then structured as follows: • Random ID (28.2%) A conventional held-out baseline drawn from the remaining in-distribution pool. • Seen-Pattern ID (18.9%) Unseen pairs whose CWE classes and specific patch-diff clusters were already observed during training. • Same-CWE New-Pattern OOD (21.1%) Isolates pattern-level generalization. The CWE class is known, but the specific patch-diff cluster is entirely withheld from training. • Project OOD (17.5%) Measures cross-project robustness by withholding complete repositories (e.g. krb5, postgres) from training ( Steenhoek et al., 2023 ) . • Temporal OOD (14.3%) Isolates later Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records (disclosed in 2024) to simulate future deployment and prevent temporal leakage ( Jimenez et al., 2019 ) . Evaluation groups are extracted through a strict priority cascade that withholds full projects first, then temporal CVEs from the remaining data, and finally unseen pattern clusters. This sequential partitioning prevents samples from satisfying multiple holdout conditions simultaneously, with automated checks verifying zero leakage across splits. 2.4. Evaluation Metrics Due to the balanced paired design, Accuracy serves as the primary classification metric, complemented by the F1 score. Because the negative class consists exclusively of repaired code, the Patch False-Positive Rate (Patch-FPR) is explicitly evaluated. A high Patch-FPR indicates that the model frequently flags repaired code as vulnerable, failing to recognize the security fix. Symmetrically, the False-Negative Rate (FNR) measures the proportion of genuine vulnerabilities that the model misses. For OOD detection and distance-based risk, the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) is used. Each sample receives a continuous distance score reflecting its geometric displacement from the training ID Core toward unfamiliar OOD regions (Fig. 1 ), formally defined in Section 3.3 . AUROC evaluates the score’s ability to rank unfamiliar samples or incorrect predictions higher than familiar ones, independent of an operational threshold ( Fawcett, 2006 ) . 3. Methodology The experimental design evaluates embedding calibration, OOD scoring, and cross-model failure prediction. We examine two distinct model families, namely the CodeBERT encoder and the Qwen2.5-Coder language model. To isolate how task-specific training alters latent geometry compared to raw pretraining, we evaluate CodeBERT in both its original pretrained state and after fine-tuning with a joint cross-entropy and contrastive objective. The encoder produces fixed-dimensional embeddings for distance-based OOD scoring, while Qwen2.5-Coder acts as an independent generative classifier. This configuration allows us to test cross-model transfer, determining whether geometric distance scores derived from a lightweight encoder can reliably warn of prediction failures in a separate large language model. 3.1. Model and Training Setup The encoder architecture is based on CodeBERT ( microsoft/codebert-base ) ( Feng et al., 2020 ) . A central challenge in hard-negative vulnerability detection is that a vulnerable function and its patched counterpart share extensive syntactic overlap, yet a standard cross-entropy objective does not explicitly enforce geometric separation between their latent representations. To address this, the encoder is fine-tuned with a joint Cross-Entropy (CE) and Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL) objective ( Gunel et al., 2021 ; Khosla et al., 2020 ) . We adapted the contrastive loss formulation from framework implementations such as SCL-CVD and MCL-VD ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . Unlike approaches that fuse Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), control-flow graphs, or synthesized comments to optimize raw benchmark metrics, we restrict our encoder to unimodal source code. This eliminates parsing artifacts and confounders from external static analyzers, ensuring that observed geometric boundaries and neighbourhood structures directly reflect the latent properties of the contextualized language model itself. Following ( Gunel et al., 2021 ) , the optimization objective is defined as: ℒ = ℒ CE + λ ​ ℒ SCL \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SCL}} where ℒ CE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} is the standard cross-entropy classification loss. Here, I ≡ { 1 , … , N } I\equiv\{1,\dots,N\} indexes the mini-batch, where N = 8 N=8 represents the maximum batch size accommodated by GPU accelerator memory under full 512-token sequences. Ground-truth labels are denoted by y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} (vulnerable vs. patched), P ⁡ ( i ) ≡ { p ∈ A ⁡ ( i ) ∣ y p = y i } P(i)\equiv\{p\in A(i)\mid y_{p}=y_{i}\} is the set of positive indices sharing the anchor label, and A ⁡ ( i ) ≡ I ∖ { i } A(i)\equiv I\setminus\{i\} . Following common practice in contrastive learning, the temperature is set to τ = 0.07 \tau=0.07 ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Khosla et al., 2020 ) , while, following the objective-balancing principles of Gunel et al. ( Gunel et al., 2021 ) and SCL-CVD ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , the scaling weight is set to λ = 0.05 \lambda=0.05 . Training utilizes pair-complete mini-batches containing four exact vulnerable-patch pairs. This operationalizes contrastive hard-negative principles ( Robinson et al., 2021 ) by guaranteeing that the most informative counterpart, namely the repaired patch ( Xiao et al., 2020 ) , is present in every optimization step despite the hardware-constrained batch size. Both encoder variants are adapted with LoRA ( r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 , dropout 0.1 0.1 , applied to query, key, value, and dense projection modules) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , building on recent empirical evidence showing that parameter-efficient adaptation preserves foundational representations while effectively capturing code task semantics ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . The final three transformer layers are additionally unfrozen, preserving general pretrained structure in lower layers while enabling task-specific abstraction in upper layers ( Lee et al., 2019 ) . As a cross-model reliability baseline, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct ( Hui et al., 2024 ) is adapted as a sequence classifier via QLoRA (4-bit NF4, r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 , dropout 0.05 0.05 ) ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Shestov et al., 2025 ) . The model input consists of a specific task instruction followed directly by the C or C++ code snippet: “Analyze the following C/C++ code and determine if it contains a vulnerability.” A binary classification head is applied to the final non-padding token of this combined sequence at the output layer. The LLM is fine-tuned using standard cross-entropy loss, where a pair-preserving sampler places vulnerable and patched counterparts within the same mini-batch to ensure balanced gradient updates across identical project contexts. 3.2. Embedding Extraction & Calibration Embeddings are extracted from the [CLS] token ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) at every transformer layer (0–12) and as aggregated layer means. Layer choice is treated as an empirical factor because prior probing work shows a functional progression where lower layers encode general syntax, while higher layers specialize toward the training objective ( Tenney et al., 2019 ) . A final layer tightly specialized for CE classification may lose the broader distributional structure required for OOD ranking. Raw contextualized embeddings suffer from inherent anisotropy, clustering within a narrow cone of dominant directions ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) . In hard-negative vulnerability detection, where a function and its patch often differ by merely a few tokens (e.g., an added boundary check), this geometric distortion is critical: high-variance dimensions corresponding to surface syntax or project-specific identifier naming drown out the subtle semantic delta of the actual fix. To restore metric expressiveness, we apply a whitening transformation ( Su et al., 2021 ) that centers and decorrelates the training distribution via the empirical covariance 𝚺 = 𝐔 ​ 𝚲 ​ 𝐔 ⊤ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^{\top} : 𝐖 = ( 𝚲 + ϵ 𝐈 ) − 1 / 2 𝐔 ⊤ , 𝐳 white ( x ) = 𝐖 ( 𝐡 ( x ) − 𝝁 ) \mathbf{W}=(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}+\epsilon\mathbf{I})^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{white}}(x)=\mathbf{W}\bigl(\mathbf{h}(x)-\boldsymbol{\mu}\bigr) where 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} is the training mean vector and ϵ = 10 − 5 \epsilon=10^{-5} is a numerical regularizer. By equalizing eigenvalue variance across all feature dimensions, whitening prevents generic code structure from dominating cosine similarity, allowing localized repair semantics to govern latent distances. 3.3. Distance-Based OOD Scoring Vulnerability data is multi-modal, with different CWE classes, projects, and patch patterns occupying distinct local regions in the embedding space. Consequently, OOD scoring is operationalized using a non-parametric k k -nearest-neighbour cosine distance to the training distribution ( Sun et al., 2022 ) . Let E ⁡ ( x ) E(x) denote the calibrated embedding of sample x x under a given transformation (e.g., E ​ ( x ) = 𝐳 white ​ ( x ) E(x)=\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{white}}(x) ), and let N k ​ ( x ) N_{k}(x) denote its set of k k nearest training neighbours under cosine similarity. The non-parametric outlier score is computed as: OOD k ​ ( x ) = 1 − 1 k ​ ∑ n i ∈ N k ​ ( x ) cos ⁡ ( E ⁡ ( x ) , E ⁡ ( n i ) ) \mathrm{OOD}_{k}(x)=1-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{n_{i}\in N_{k}(x)}\cos\bigl(E(x),\,E(n_{i})\bigr) The parameter k k is systematically swept across k ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 , 50 , 100 } k\in\{1,3,5,10,20,30,50,100\} . A diagonal approximation of the class-conditional Mahalanobis distance ( Lee et al., 2018 ) is included as a global parametric baseline. To evaluate whether distance scores expose a gradual generalization boundary, test samples are grouped into ten equal-frequency distance bins to compute accuracy and error rates. This is evaluated intrinsically (the encoder scored against its own predictions) and cross-model (using encoder-derived distances to rank LLM errors). Because neural networks can remain overconfident under distribution shift ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) , the LLM’s internal confidence (maximum softmax probability) ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ) is reported as a baseline. The analysis is repeated across shift types (in-distribution, unseen-pattern, cross-project, temporal), additionally measuring pair-exact correctness to assess whether both sides of a hard-negative pair are successfully identified. 3.4. Vulnerable-Neighbourhood Proximity A specific hard-negative failure mode occurs when a patched function remains geometrically closer to vulnerable training examples than to safe counterparts, leading to misclassification. To investigate this, we analyze patched test samples using the fine-tuned CE+SCL encoder, contrasting patched false positives (predicted vulnerable) against patched true negatives (predicted patched). The contrastive objective makes this neighbourhood-based analysis directly interpretable by explicitly shaping class-wise structure ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) . To examine how test samples interact with the underlying training distribution, proximity to the vulnerable class is quantified using four complementary metrics in the calibrated embedding space. These include a centroid margin ratio, a nearest-neighbour margin, a class-conditional k k -neighbourhood margin ratio ( k = 10 k=10 ), and the vulnerable-neighbour share among the top 10 neighbours illustrated in Fig. 2 . Grounded in neighbourhood-based prediction support and embedding similarity ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ; Shimmi et al., 2024 ) , class-conditional density estimation ( Lee et al., 2018 ) , and internal-state risk assessment ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , these metrics measure whether a patch is drawn toward the vulnerable or the safe training distribution. We assess their diagnostic value by comparing group means with 95% confidence intervals, ranking false alarms via AUROC, and evaluating risk gradients across proximity deciles. 4. While Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL) yields substantial gains in vision and NLP, its impact on raw binary classification here remains constrained. The bottleneck lies in the extreme syntactic overlap of hard-negative pairs: while SCL does not noticeably improve global OOD ranking over the raw encoder (RQ1), it successfully structures the latent space for local, class-conditional diagnostics of patched false positives (RQ3), even though translating this realignment into a superior linear decision boundary remains challenging. 4.1. RQ2: Generalization Boundaries RQ2 investigates whether embedding-based distance exposes a reliability gradient and whether this gradient behaves uniformly across distribution shifts. All following analyses use the layer-3 whitened configuration ( k = 1 k=1 ) identified in RQ1. For interpretability, the test set is divided into ten equal-frequency distance bins (169 samples each) wherever a bin-level analysis is reported. Encoder-Intrinsic and Cross-Model Boundaries Figure 4 shows CodeBERT CE+SCL performance over its own embedding distance. A clear degradation pattern emerges. Accuracy falls from 0.834 in the lowest-distance bin to 0.479 in the highest, which is a drop of more than 35 percentage points, while the patch false-positive rate rises from 0.167 to 0.631. Converting prediction correctness into a binary error indicator, the resulting error-ranking AUROC is 0.593 (Spearman r = 0.157 r=0.157 ). This confirms a modest but meaningful reliability signal consistent with the large accuracy drop (full ten-bin results available in the online replication package). Operationally, this geometric gradient enables prediction and risk-aware triage in software security pipelines. By grouping distance bins into empirical zones—Safe (Bins 1–3), Boundary (Bins 4–6), and Danger (Bins 7–10)—a system can selectively abstain from fully automated decisions on distant code. Abstaining on samples in the highest-distance Danger Zone yields 71.6% accuracy on the retained low-distance code (Safe Zone) compared to 53.4% in the rejected region (Danger Zone), while reducing the false alarm rate on safe code down to 33.7%. To evaluate whether this geometric signal transfers across model families, Figure 5 uses raw CodeBERT distance to rank errors made by the independently fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder LLM. LLM accuracy decreases from 0.680 to 0.539 across distance bins, while mean confidence declines only slightly from ≈ \approx 0.81 to ≈ \approx 0.78. This reproduces the known overconfidence of neural networks under distribution shift ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ) . While the cross-model error-ranking AUROC (0.556) is weaker than the encoder-intrinsic setting, it remains consistently above random ranking. CodeBERT distance and LLM confidence thus capture complementary reliability aspects: confidence reflects internal certainty, while distance provides an external measure of distributional proximity.
